title: SRE fieldplay: throttle & stream hiccups
content:
Purpose:
This is a compact, field-ready SRE primer (a.k.a. 'fieldplay') for the most common API service degradations we keep hitting: backend timeouts, client 429s, degraded streaming/partial responses, and sudden spike in error rates. Goal is: give oncall a set of fast checks and mitigations that are low-friction and reversible.

Status: draft, iterative. Notes to self: verify that alert thresholds in ops-monitoring match the ranges below. Add circuit-breaker knobs for the streaming worker pool (TODO).

Quick summary of failure modes we care about:
- Timeouts: request processing exceeds caller SLOs (often seen as 5xx w/ upstream timeout code path).
- 429s (rate-limited): client-facing rate limiter or downstream throttling (upstream capacity loss -> cascading 429s).
- Streaming degradation: partial frames, stalled chunks, reconnect loops (clients see stalled progress or truncated outputs).
- Elevated error rates: sudden increase in 5xx/4xx error surface across routes (can be a buggy deploy, bad config, or infra flapping).

Detection signals (fast things to glance at):
- Grafana overview: 1) p95/p99 latency spike across endpoints, 2) incoming request 429 rate, 3) streaming ack/byte-rate drop, 4) error-rate per route (5xx/sec).
- Recent deploys: check release-engineering/CI pipeline for merges in last 30 mins.
- Autoscaler events: node pool scale-in/scale-out or GKE preemption history.
- Backfill metrics: backend queue length, fine-grained worker saturation, KV cache hit rate.

Immediate triage checklist (first 10 minutes) - do these in parallel where possible:
1) Verify symptoms: reproduce a failing request via curl/postman from the same region where users report issues. Capture exact error (timeout, 429 payload, truncated stream) and timestamp.
2) Check alerts graph panel and Top Talkers dashboard to confirm scope (single route, single region, global).
3) Look at last deploy and rollout status: is a canary failing? Is traffic shifted to a new revision? (linked: github PR and rollout id).
4) If 429s: determine origin of the 429 token - our edge vs internal rate limiter vs third-party. Query rate-limiter logs (rlm) for token bucket exhaustion.
5) If streaming degraded: tail streaming worker logs (grep "stream: drop" / "kv-cache-miss") for patterns; check connection churn and websocket error counts.
6) If timeout spikes: inspect upstream RPC latencies and database slow query logs. Check KV cache eviction bursts.
7) If error-rate rises broadly: consider an immediate rollback to previous stable revision (see rollback section).

Fast mitigations (playbook by symptom):
- Timeouts:
  * Short-term: temporarily increase request timeout on edge (if safe) to avoid client-side retries creating load; enable 503 fallback to cached responses for high-QPS read routes.
  * Medium: reduce max-concurrency per worker (pressure-release) and enable burst routing to dedicated pool if available.
  * Long-term: add more fine-grained latency histograms and per-shard tracing.

- 429s (rate limiting):
  * Short-term: widen global token bucket or bump soft-limits for internal service-to-service calls. For customer-facing 429s, enable degraded response path that returns a short stub result + retry-after header.
  * If rate-limiter backing store is slow (redis/Tikv): point rate-limiter to read-only fallback or enable local leaky-bucket approximation.
  * Medium-term: implement smarter per-customer backpressure and circuit-breaker with degrade-to-embedding-only mode.

- Streaming degradation:
  * Short-term: force clients to one-shot mode (disable streaming) via a feature-flag gate at the edge to reduce long-lived connection pressure.
  * Rotate worker pools handling streaming (drain and recreate VMs) if per-process memory grows and GC pauses correlate.
  * Check KV cache hit rate: if prefix cache missed heavily, prime cache with hot prefixes.

- Elevated error rates:
  * Short-term: identify suspect revision and rollback canary. Put rate-limiting on newly deployed route.
  * If dependent service failing: switch to degraded fallback (cached responses, stub outputs), mark incident as "partial-degradation".

Escalation and ownership:
- Pager flow: oncall -> SRE lead -> runtime-owner -> product eng if evidence points to model/response regressions.
- Use Slack channel #sre-oncall and tag with the incident shorthand (e.g., "fieldplay: throttles-2024-12-12").
- If more than 30 min to mitigation, set SEV level and loop in support/CS for customer messaging.

Rollback & traffic control patterns (how to quickly get back to stable):
- Prefer traffic rollback over risky hot-fixes for widespread regressions. Use rollout dashboard to shift traffic to last-green revision (30% -> 100% in 10m increments).
- If rollback not possible (stateful migrations), apply selective route rate-limiting and re-route high-QPS customers to dedicated capacity.

Instrumentation & queries to run (cheat sheet):
- Query: 5xx_count by route, region (past 15m).
- Query: 429_rate by client_api_key (top 20).
- Query: streaming_byte_rate per connection (p95) and websocket_reconnect_count.
- Check: redis latency (p95/p99), worker GC pause histogram, CPU steal on nodes.

Common pitfalls / gotchas:
- "Fixing" timeouts by increasing global timeouts often hides root cause and amplifies load with slow requests. Prefer backpressure + cached fallbacks.
- 429s observed at the edge can be from downstream slow storage—ensure rate-limiter origin annotations are enabled in logs.
- Client retries without jitter are a major multiplier; enforce retry-after and server-side retry budget.

Field notes / recent lessons (freeform):
- 2024-09: observed repeated streaming stalls when a model shard OOMs quietly; GC pauses on python worker coincided with lost frames. Solution: added memory headroom and safer stream chunking.
- 2024-10: global 429 surge traced to a misconfigured SaaS customer sending bursts during their nightly batch; we added per-customer burst windows.

Post-incident followups (action items):
- Add synthetic streaming probe from each region (tickets: JIRA-SRE-842).
- Instrument rate-limiter to emit origin context (edge vs service).
- Add canary-level traffic shaping toggle in Console for faster targeted rollbacks.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Should we allow oncall to flip the streaming feature-flag via Console? (security/permission check)
- Can we safely expose a degraded JSON-only mode to customers as a permanent fallback?

Appendix: quick commands
- Tail streaming logs: kubectl -n runtime logs -l app=stream-worker --since=15m | grep -E "(drop|reset|error)"
- Find top 429 sources: elasticsearch query for status:429 | top client_api_key
- Rollback: ./infra/rollout rollback --service api-gateway --to last-green

End of draft. Keep short, actionable, and add more concrete playbook snippets after next DR drill.
